subject: Neurology
vignette: A 45-year-old man develops progressive headache, nausea, and papilledema 3 weeks after treatment for bacterial meningitis. Imaging shows dilation of all four ventricles with no mass or aqueductal obstruction.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this patient's condition?

options.text: Noncommunicating hydrocephalus due to aqueductal stenosis
Normal pressure hydrocephalus with the classic clinical triad
Communicating hydrocephalus due to impaired CSF absorption at arachnoid granulations
Ex vacuo ventriculomegaly from cortical atrophy

explanation_correct: Post-meningitic scarring of the arachnoid granulations reduces CSF absorption, producing communicating hydrocephalus. Because the CSF pathways within the ventricles remain patent, all ventricles are dilated. Impaired absorption raises intracranial pressure, leading to headache, papilledema, and potentially herniation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Noncommunicating hydrocephalus results from a structural blockage within the ventricular system and dilates only ventricles upstream of the obstruction.
explanation_incorrect.B: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is an idiopathic disorder of older adults with gait apraxia, cognitive dysfunction, and urinary incontinence and normal CSF pressure.
explanation_incorrect.D: Ex vacuo ventriculomegaly reflects brain tissue loss from atrophy, has normal intracranial pressure, and is not associated with papilledema.
explanation_incorrect.E: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension has elevated pressure but normal-sized ventricles and no structural lesion on imaging.

educationalObjective: Distinguish communicating hydrocephalus with dilation of all ventricles from obstructive and ex vacuo causes.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 72-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of a broad-based, shuffling gait described as magnetic, mild cognitive decline, and new urinary incontinence. Imaging shows ventriculomegaly without prominent sulcal enlargement. CSF opening pressure is normal on measurement.
question: Which of the following best describes the underlying pathology in this patient?

options.text: Obstructive hydrocephalus from a colloid cyst
Normal pressure hydrocephalus with episodically elevated CSF pressure distorting corona radiata fibers
Alzheimer disease with ex vacuo ventriculomegaly

explanation_correct: Normal pressure hydrocephalus affects older adults and presents with the triad of gait apraxia (magnetic gait), cognitive dysfunction, and urinary incontinence, remembered as wobbly, wacky, and wet. CSF pressure is elevated only episodically. Ventricular expansion distorts the corona radiata fibers, producing the characteristic gait and cognitive findings, and treatment is CSF drainage by lumbar puncture or shunt.

explanation_incorrect.A: A colloid cyst causes obstructive hydrocephalus with positional headache and isolated upstream ventricular dilation, not this chronic triad.
explanation_incorrect.C: Alzheimer disease produces ex vacuo ventriculomegaly with sulcal enlargement and dementia but not gait apraxia or incontinence as a defining triad.
explanation_incorrect.D: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension occurs in younger patients with headache, papilledema, and normal-sized ventricles rather than ventriculomegaly.
explanation_incorrect.E: A chronic subdural hematoma causes headache and focal deficits with a crescentic collection rather than a symmetric ventriculomegaly and classic triad.

educationalObjective: Identify the wobbly, wacky, wet triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus and its corona radiata mechanism.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 78-year-old man with a history of Alzheimer disease undergoes imaging that shows enlarged ventricles. He has no gait apraxia, no incontinence, and no acute change from his baseline dementia. His CSF opening pressure is normal.
question: Which of the following best explains the ventricular enlargement in this patient?

options.text: Communicating hydrocephalus from impaired arachnoid granulation absorption
Ex vacuo ventriculomegaly due to brain tissue atrophy

explanation_correct: Ex vacuo ventriculomegaly refers to increased CSF space on imaging due to decreased brain tissue from neuronal atrophy, as in Alzheimer disease, HIV, frontotemporal dementia, or Huntington disease. Intracranial pressure is normal and the normal pressure hydrocephalus triad is absent. This is a mimic of hydrocephalus rather than a true CSF circulation or absorption disorder.

explanation_incorrect.A: Communicating hydrocephalus raises intracranial pressure and causes papilledema with dilation of all ventricles, not a normal-pressure atrophic process.
explanation_incorrect.B: Noncommunicating hydrocephalus dilates ventricles upstream of a structural obstruction and would not be explained by cortical atrophy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Normal pressure hydrocephalus requires the gait, cognitive, and urinary triad, which this patient does not have beyond his baseline dementia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension produces normal-sized ventricles with papilledema and headache in younger patients.

educationalObjective: Differentiate ex vacuo ventriculomegaly from true hydrocephalus by normal pressure and absence of the NPH triad.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 35-year-old woman presents with severe positional headache and episodic loss of consciousness. Imaging reveals a hyperdense mass at the foramen of Monro with marked dilation of the lateral ventricles but normal-sized third and fourth ventricles.
question: Where is the most likely site of CSF flow obstruction?
explanation_correct: A colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro causes noncommunicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus by blocking CSF outflow from the lateral ventricles. Only the ventricles upstream of the obstruction, the lateral ventricles, become dilated, while the third and fourth ventricles remain normal in size. Positional headache and intermittent loss of consciousness are classic features.

explanation_incorrect.B: Aqueductal stenosis would dilate both the lateral and third ventricles while sparing only the fourth ventricle.
explanation_incorrect.C: Arachnoid granulation dysfunction causes communicating hydrocephalus with dilation of all ventricles rather than isolated lateral ventricular enlargement.
explanation_incorrect.D: The foramen magnum is not a typical intraventricular CSF pathway obstruction and would not selectively dilate the lateral ventricles.
explanation_incorrect.E: Obstruction at the fourth ventricular outlet would cause dilation of all ventricles upstream, including the fourth ventricle.

educationalObjective: Localize an obstructive hydrocephalus lesion based on which ventricles are dilated upstream of the blockage.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A newborn presents with an enlarging head circumference and a bulging fontanelle. Imaging shows marked dilation of the lateral and third ventricles with a normal-sized fourth ventricle. No mass lesion is identified.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this ventricular dilation?

options.text: Colloid cyst of the third ventricle
Stenosis of the aqueduct of Sylvius

explanation_correct: Stenosis of the aqueduct of Sylvius is a classic cause of noncommunicating hydrocephalus in newborns. Because the obstruction lies between the third and fourth ventricles, the lateral and third ventricles dilate upstream while the fourth ventricle remains normal. This is the most common congenital form of obstructive hydrocephalus.

explanation_incorrect.A: Post-meningitic arachnoid scarring impairs absorption at the arachnoid granulations and produces communicating hydrocephalus with all ventricles dilated.
explanation_incorrect.B: A colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro would dilate only the lateral ventricles, not the third ventricle.
explanation_incorrect.C: A choroid plexus papilloma causes hydrocephalus by CSF overproduction, producing a communicating pattern with all ventricles dilated.
explanation_incorrect.E: Ex vacuo ventriculomegaly results from brain atrophy with normal pressure and does not present with an enlarging head in a newborn.

educationalObjective: Recognize aqueductal stenosis as a cause of congenital noncommunicating hydrocephalus with lateral and third ventricular dilation.
